title: Migrations in CI/CD
summary: Why EnsureCreated and Migrate() at start-up do not belong in production, idempotent scripts and bundles, catching forgotten migrations in CI, and the rename that drops a column.

steps.title: How schema changes reach production
body: Earlier exercises called `EnsureCreated()` at start-up. It creates the schema if the database is empty and does **nothing** otherwise: it cannot add a column to a live database, and it skips the migrations history, so you can never switch to migrations later without trouble. Fine for tests and demos, never for production.

`context.Database.Migrate()` at start-up does apply migrations, but it is still risky in production: with three instances starting together they race (EF Core 9 added a lock against concurrent migrations, but not every provider and setup is covered), the app's login needs rights to alter tables, a failed migration crashes the app on boot, and nobody reviewed the SQL.
The usual pipeline instead:
```bash fragment
# in CI, on every pull request: fail if someone changed the model but forgot the migration
dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes
# in the release build: one SQL script that is safe to run against any version of the database
dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent --output artifacts/migrate.sql
# or a self-contained executable that applies them, for the deploy step
dotnet ef migrations bundle --self-contained -r linux-x64 --output artifacts/efbundle
./efbundle --connection "$DB_CONNECTION"

`--idempotent` wraps each migration in a check against `__EFMigrationsHistory`, so the same script works whether the database is one migration behind or ten. The deploy applies the script (or bundle) **before** the new app version starts, and the migrations are written so the **old** version still works with the new schema while both run (add a column first, drop the old one in a later release).

steps.prompt: Put the release pipeline for a schema change in order.
lines: Developer runs dotnet ef migrations add and reviews the generated code
CI fails the build if dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes finds model changes with no migration
Release build produces migrate.sql with dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent
A reviewer (or DBA) reads the SQL
The deploy applies migrate.sql to the database
The deploy rolls out the new version of the app

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it is for.
pairs: generate a new migration from the model changes
one SQL script safe to run on a database at any migration
an executable that applies pending migrations
move a dev database to exactly that migration (up or down)
delete the last migration, if it was never applied

steps.prompt: The API runs as 4 instances. A teammate adds `db.Database.Migrate();` to `Program.cs` "so deploys are simpler". What is your review comment?
options: Apply migrations in a deploy step (idempotent script or bundle) before the new version starts; the app's login should not need ALTER rights, and a failed migration should not crash every instance on boot
Fine, as long as it runs inside a transaction
Only call it when `app.Environment.IsProduction()` is true
steps.explain: It works on a laptop, which is why it slips through review. In production it ties schema changes to app start-up: four instances race (or wait on a lock), the app needs owner rights, and nobody saw the SQL before it ran.

steps.title: The rename that drops a column
body: You rename `Venue.Name` to `Title` and run `dotnet ef migrations add RenameVenueNameToTitle`. EF Core cannot tell a rename from "one property removed, another added", so it may scaffold this, and says so:
```text
An operation was scaffolded that may result in the loss of data. Please review the migration for accuracy.
```csharp fragment
migrationBuilder.DropColumn(name: "Name", table: "Venues");
migrationBuilder.AddColumn<string>(name: "Title", table: "Venues", nullable: false, defaultValue: "");
Applied to production, every venue loses its name. That warning is the reason to **read every generated migration** and the SQL script. The fix is to edit the migration by hand:
```csharp fragment
migrationBuilder.RenameColumn(name: "Name", table: "Venues", newName: "Title");
Edit migrations freely before they are applied anywhere shared; once applied, add a new migration instead.

steps.title: Save the venue names
prompt: Two migrations are written out in full (`dotnet ef` cannot run here, so they are hand-written classes, exactly like the generated ones). The program deletes the database, applies both with `Migrate()` and prints every venue's title.

Right now it prints three empty lines: the second migration drops `Name` and adds an empty `Title`. Fix **that migration** so the data survives: the program must print `Pier Hall`, `Chapel Rooms` and `Dockside Arena`.

tests.name: the venues keep their names after the migration

hints: Replace the DropColumn and AddColumn calls with one call.
steps.explain: On SQL Server this becomes `EXEC sp_rename`, on PostgreSQL and SQLite `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN`. With several app instances running old code, a rename still breaks the old version: the zero-downtime way is add `Title`, copy, deploy code that reads `Title`, and drop `Name` in a later release.

steps.prompt: The release job needs one script that works against staging (2 migrations behind) and production (5 behind).
steps.explain: Without `--idempotent` the script starts from an empty database (migration 0) by default, so it fails on any database that already has some of the migrations.

steps.prompt: An integration test against a fresh database fails with this. What happened?
code: System.InvalidOperationException: An error was generated for warning
has pending changes. Add a new migration before updating the database.
options: Someone changed an entity or the model configuration but did not add a migration; run `dotnet ef migrations add` and commit it
The database server is too old
The test should call `EnsureCreated()` instead of `MigrateAsync()`
Suppress the warning with `ConfigureWarnings` and move on
steps.explain: Since EF Core 9 this is an error by default: the model no longer matches the last migration snapshot, so migrating would leave the database out of date. CI should catch it earlier with `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes`. (The exercises here suppress it only because their migrations are hand-written without a snapshot.)
